LECTURE 22 Stage 4: Architecture

The Transformer Block

Combining Multi-Head Attention, Feed-Forward Networks, Layer Normalization, and Residual Connections into One Repeatable Unit
50 min read Advanced The fundamental building block of every modern LLM

Introduction: From Components to a Complete Block

Over the last several lectures, we have built four critical components one by one:

  • Multi-Head Causal Self-Attention (Lectures 13-18) — allows each token to attend to previous tokens through multiple parallel attention heads
  • Feed-Forward Network with GELU (Lecture 19) — applies a non-linear transformation independently to each token position
  • Layer Normalization (Lecture 20) — stabilizes training by normalizing activation statistics
  • Residual Connections (Lecture 21) — create information highways that allow gradients to flow through deep networks

Each of these components, on its own, solves one specific problem. But the magic of the Transformer architecture is how they are combined. In this lecture, we will assemble them into the Transformer Block — the single, repeatable unit that gets stacked to create GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, LLaMA, and virtually every modern language model.

Key Insight: A Transformer Block is like a LEGO brick. Each brick is identical in structure. But by stacking many of them, you can build anything from a simple wall to an elaborate castle. Similarly, GPT-2 Small stacks 12 identical Transformer Blocks; GPT-3 stacks 96. The same block design, repeated, produces emergent capabilities that no single block could achieve alone.

The Pre-Norm Transformer Block Architecture

There are two main variants of the Transformer Block, differing in where Layer Normalization is applied:

  • Post-Norm (original 2017 Transformer): Apply LayerNorm after the residual addition
  • Pre-Norm (GPT-2 and most modern LLMs): Apply LayerNorm before the sub-layer

We will implement the Pre-Norm variant, which is what GPT-2 uses and what has become the standard in modern practice. Pre-Norm is more stable during training because the residual path remains "clean" — the main signal passes through without being distorted by normalization.

The Two Sub-Layers

A Transformer Block consists of exactly two sub-layers, each wrapped with a residual connection:

Transformer Block (Pre-Norm)

Sub-Layer 1: Attention

x = x + MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm(x))

Sub-Layer 2: Feed-Forward

x = x + FeedForward(LayerNorm(x))

Let us trace exactly what happens step by step:

  1. Input x arrives with shape (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
  2. LayerNorm1(x) — normalize across the d_model dimension
  3. MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm1(x)) — compute attention; output has same shape
  4. x = x + attention_output — residual connection adds the original input back
  5. LayerNorm2(x) — normalize again (using a different LayerNorm with its own parameters)
  6. FeedForward(LayerNorm2(x)) — expand to 4×d_model, apply GELU, project back to d_model
  7. x = x + ffn_output — second residual connection
  8. Output x with shape (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) — same shape as input!
Analogy: The Transformer Block as an Expert Committee

Think of a Transformer Block as a two-phase committee review process. In the first phase (attention), each committee member looks at what everyone else has said and gathers relevant context. In the second phase (feed-forward), each member independently processes what they learned, applying their own deep expertise to form a refined opinion. The residual connections are like keeping your original notes — even after hearing from others and thinking deeply, you do not discard your initial understanding; you add to it.

Why This Specific Order Matters

The order — attention first, then feed-forward — is not arbitrary. There is a deep conceptual reason:

  • Attention is a communication mechanism. It allows tokens to share information across positions. After attention, each token's representation is a mixture of information from itself and other tokens in the sequence.
  • Feed-Forward is a computation mechanism. It processes each token's representation independently, applying learned transformations. It takes the mixed information from attention and "thinks" about it.

This creates a powerful pattern: communicate, then compute. Communicate, then compute. Each block refines the representations by first gathering context and then processing it.

Research Perspective: Anthropic's research on mechanistic interpretability has shown that these two sub-layers perform fundamentally different functions. Attention heads develop specialized roles like "induction heads" (pattern matching) and "position heads" (tracking relative positions), while feed-forward layers act as key-value memories that store factual knowledge. The combination is what makes Transformers so powerful.

Assembling the Transformer Block

Let us now implement a complete Transformer Block in NumPy. We will include each sub-component (which we built in previous lectures) and combine them into a single, clean TransformerBlock class. Notice how simple the assembly is — all the complexity is hidden inside each component:

Python

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# (Component classes defined as above)
class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-5):
 self.gamma = np.ones(d_model)
 self.beta = np.zeros(d_model)
 self.eps = eps
 def forward(self, x):
 mean = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 var = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.n_heads = n_heads
 self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
 scale = np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.W_q = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_k = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_v = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_o = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x @ self.W_q).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 K = (x @ self.W_k).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 V = (x @ self.W_v).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 scores = Q @ K.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2) / np.sqrt(self.head_dim)
 mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1) * (-1e9)
 scores = scores + mask
 exp_s = np.exp(scores - np.max(scores, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
 attn = exp_s / np.sum(exp_s, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 out = (attn @ V).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, T, C)
 return out @ self.W_o

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):
 d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d_model, d_ff) / np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(d_ff)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(d_ff, d_model) / np.sqrt(d_ff)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d_model)
 def gelu(self, x):
 return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x**3)))
 def forward(self, x):
 return self.gelu(x @ self.W1 + self.b1) @ self.W2 + self.b2

# ============================================================
# THE TRANSFORMER BLOCK - The core repeatable unit
# ============================================================
class TransformerBlock:
 """A single Transformer block using Pre-Norm architecture (GPT-2 style).

 Architecture:
 x -> LayerNorm -> MultiHeadAttention -> + (residual) ->
 -> LayerNorm -> FeedForward -> + (residual) -> output
 """
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before attention
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads) # Multi-head attention
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before FFN
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model) # Feed-forward network

 def forward(self, x):
 # Sub-layer 1: LayerNorm -> Attention -> Residual Add
 attn_output = self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + attn_output # Residual connection

 # Sub-layer 2: LayerNorm -> FFN -> Residual Add
 ffn_output = self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 x = x + ffn_output # Residual connection

 return x

# Test the Transformer Block
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
batch_size = 2
seq_len = 8

block = TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads)
x = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, d_model)

print(f"Transformer Block Configuration:")
print(f" d_model = {d_model}")
print(f" n_heads = {n_heads}")
print(f" head_dim = {d_model // n_heads}")
print(f" d_ff = {4 * d_model}")
print()

print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
output = block.forward(x)
print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
print(f"Shape preserved: {x.shape == output.shape}")
print()

# Verify the output is different from input (the block did something!)
diff = np.mean(np.abs(output - x))
print(f"Mean absolute change: {diff:.6f}")
print(f"This confirms the block is processing the data, not just passing it through.")

Look at that! The input shape (2, 8, 64) equals the output shape (2, 8, 64). This is the critical property that allows stacking: every Transformer Block takes in a tensor of shape (batch, seq_len, d_model) and outputs a tensor of exactly the same shape. This means we can chain as many blocks as we want, each one refining the representations further.

A Token's Journey Through the Block

Let us trace what happens to a single token (say, at position 2) as it passes through the Transformer Block:

  1. LayerNorm — The token's representation is normalized to zero mean, unit variance
  2. Attention — The token attends to positions [0, 1, 2] (causal mask blocks position 3+). It computes a weighted sum of values, gathering context from earlier tokens
  3. Residual Add — The original representation is added back, preserving what the token already "knew"
  4. LayerNorm — Normalize again with a separate set of parameters
  5. FFN — Expand to 4×d_model, apply GELU, project back. This is independent "thinking" at each position
  6. Residual Add — Again, add back the representation from before the FFN

After one block, the token's representation contains: (a) its original information, (b) contextual information from other tokens, and (c) nonlinear transformations of the combined information. Its meaning has been enriched while its identity is preserved.

Analogy: A Student in a Study Group

Consider a student (token at position 2) studying for an exam. First, they listen to what study partners have to say and weigh contributions by relevance (attention). They do not forget what they already knew (residual add). Then they think deeply and independently about what they have learned (FFN), again without discarding accumulated knowledge (residual add). After multiple rounds (stacked blocks), understanding becomes deep and nuanced.

Stacking Blocks: How Depth Creates Capability

A single Transformer Block can do useful work, but the real power comes from stacking. Here is what we know about how depth creates emergent capabilities:

DepthWhat the Model Can LearnExample
1-2 blocksSimple pattern matching, bigram/trigram statistics"The cat sat on the ___" → "mat"
4-6 blocksSyntactic structure, basic grammar rulesSubject-verb agreement across distance
8-12 blocksSemantic understanding, factual recall"The capital of France is ___" → "Paris"
24-48 blocksComplex reasoning, in-context learningFollowing instructions, few-shot learning
96+ blocksEmergent abilities: chain-of-thought, analogical reasoningMulti-step math, code generation
Key Insight: Each block does not need to learn everything. Early blocks tend to learn syntactic features (grammar, word order), middle blocks learn semantic features (meaning, relationships), and late blocks learn task-specific features (completing prompts, answering questions). This is similar to how layers in a CNN learn edges, then textures, then objects.

Stacking Multiple Blocks

Let us stack several Transformer Blocks and observe how the representations evolve with depth:

Python

# Compact class names used from here onward:
# LN = LayerNorm, Attn = CausalSelfAttention, FFN = FeedForward, Bk = TransformerBlock
# These are functionally identical to the verbose versions from earlier lectures.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(d), np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 m = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 v = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - m) / np.sqrt(v + 1e-5)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.h, self.hd = h, d // h
 s = np.sqrt(d)
 self.Wq = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wk = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wv = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wo = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x@self.Wq).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 K = (x@self.Wk).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 V = (x@self.Wv).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 s = Q@K.transpose(0,1,3,2)/np.sqrt(self.hd)
 s = s + np.triu(np.ones((T,T)),k=1)*(-1e9)
 e = np.exp(s - np.max(s,axis=-1,keepdims=True))
 a = e / np.sum(e,axis=-1,keepdims=True)
 return (a@V).transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(B,T,C)@self.Wo

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d,4*d)/np.sqrt(d)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(4*d)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(4*d,d)/np.sqrt(4*d)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 h = x@self.W1+self.b1
 h = 0.5*h*(1+np.tanh(np.sqrt(2/np.pi)*(h+0.044715*h**3)))
 return h@self.W2+self.b2

class TransformerBlock:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d, h)
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 x = x + self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 return x

# Stack 6 Transformer Blocks
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
n_layers = 6

blocks = [TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads) for _ in range(n_layers)]

# Input
x = np.random.randn(1, 8, d_model) * 0.02 # Small initial values (like embeddings)

print("=== Passing Data Through 6 Stacked Transformer Blocks ===")
print(f"Config: d_model={d_model}, n_heads={n_heads}, n_layers={n_layers}")
print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
print()

# Track statistics at each layer
initial_repr = x[0, 0].copy() # Track first token

for i, block in enumerate(blocks):
 x = block.forward(x)
 token_repr = x[0, 0]

 # How different is this token's repr from the original?
 cosine_sim = np.dot(initial_repr, token_repr) / (
 np.linalg.norm(initial_repr) * np.linalg.norm(token_repr) + 1e-10
 )

 print(f"After Block {i+1}:")
 print(f" Output shape: {x.shape}")
 print(f" Mean: {np.mean(x):.6f} Std: {np.std(x):.4f}")
 print(f" Cosine similarity to input: {cosine_sim:.4f}")
 print()

print("Key Observations:")
print(" 1. Shape is preserved through ALL blocks (required for stacking)")
print(" 2. The representation evolves - cosine similarity to input changes")
print(" 3. Each block transforms the representation, building on previous blocks")
print(" 4. This is exactly how GPT-2 processes text through 12 blocks")

Parameter Count of a Transformer Block

Understanding the parameter count is essential for appreciating model scale. Let us count every learnable parameter in a single Transformer Block:

Parameters in One Transformer Block

LayerNorm 1: γ (d_model) + β (d_model) = 2 × d_model

Multi-Head Attention:

  • WQ: d_model × d_model
  • WK: d_model × d_model
  • WV: d_model × d_model
  • WO: d_model × d_model
  • Total: 4 × d_model2

LayerNorm 2: 2 × d_model

Feed-Forward Network:

  • W1: d_model × 4d_model
  • b1: 4d_model
  • W2: 4d_model × d_model
  • b2: d_model
  • Total: 8 × d_model2 + 5 × d_model

Grand Total per block: 12 × d_model2 + 9 × d_model

For GPT-2 Small (d_model = 768): 12 × 7682 + 9 × 768 = 7,084,032 + 6,912 = ~7.09M parameters per block

With 12 blocks: ~85M parameters (just in the Transformer Blocks alone)

Let us verify this with code and see how parameters scale across GPT-2 variants:

Python

import numpy as np

def block_params(d_model):
 """Count parameters in one Transformer Block."""
 attn = 4 * d_model ** 2 # W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O
 ffn = 8 * d_model ** 2 + 5 * d_model # W1, b1, W2, b2
 layer_norms = 4 * d_model # 2 x (gamma + beta)
 return attn + ffn + layer_norms

# Compare model sizes
models = [
 ("Our Mini GPT", 128, 4, 4),
 ("GPT-2 Small", 768, 12, 12),
 ("GPT-2 Medium", 1024, 16, 24),
 ("GPT-2 Large", 1280, 20, 36),
 ("GPT-2 XL", 1600, 25, 48),
]

print(f"{'Model':<16} {'d_model':>7} {'Layers':>7} {'Per Block':>12} {'All Blocks':>14}")
print("-" * 60)
for name, d, heads, layers in models:
 bp = block_params(d)
 total_blocks = bp * layers
 print(f"{name:<16} {d:>7} {layers:>7} {bp:>12,} {total_blocks:>14,}")

print()
# Show ratio: FFN vs Attention parameters
d = 768
attn_p = 4 * d * d
ffn_p = 8 * d * d + 5 * d
print(f"For d_model={d}:")
print(f" Attention params per block: {attn_p:,} ({attn_p/(attn_p+ffn_p):.0%})")
print(f" FFN params per block: {ffn_p:,} ({ffn_p/(attn_p+ffn_p):.0%})")
print(f" -> The FFN has ~2x more parameters than attention!")

Why the Transformer Block Works So Well

The Transformer Block's design embodies several key principles that make it remarkably effective:

  1. Separation of concerns: Attention handles inter-token communication; FFN handles per-token computation. These are fundamentally different operations, and keeping them separate allows each to specialize.
  2. Graceful gradient flow: The residual connections ensure that gradients can flow directly from the output back to the input, even through 96+ layers. Without residuals, training such deep networks would be impossible.
  3. Stable training dynamics: Pre-norm LayerNorm ensures that the inputs to each sub-layer have well-behaved statistics (zero mean, unit variance), preventing the extreme activations that would destabilize training.
  4. Composability: Because input and output shapes match, blocks can be stacked indefinitely. This is the key to scaling — more blocks means more capacity without any architectural changes.
  5. Parallelism: Unlike RNNs, attention over the full sequence can be computed in parallel. This is what makes GPUs so effective for Transformer training.
Common Misconception

Many people think you need to understand the Transformer Block as one monolithic, complex mechanism. In reality, it is just four simple components combined in a specific pattern. If you understand LayerNorm, Attention, FFN, and Residual Connections individually, you understand the Transformer Block. There is no "fifth ingredient" — the magic is in the combination and repetition.

Summary

In this lecture, we assembled the Transformer Block — the fundamental repeatable unit of every modern LLM. We saw how:

  • The Pre-Norm architecture applies LayerNorm before each sub-layer, keeping the residual path clean
  • Sub-layer 1 (attention) handles communication between tokens
  • Sub-layer 2 (FFN) handles computation within each token
  • Residual connections preserve information and enable gradient flow
  • The input and output shapes are identical, enabling arbitrary stacking
  • Stacking creates emergent capabilities that no single block can achieve

In the next lecture, we will use these blocks to assemble the complete GPT architecture — adding token embeddings, positional embeddings, and the output projection head to create a model that can actually process text and generate predictions.

LECTURE 22 Etapa 4: Arhitectură

Lecția 22: Blocul Transformer

Combinarea Multi-Head Attention, Rețelelor Feed-Forward, Layer Normalization și Conexiunilor Reziduale într-o Singură Unitate Repetabilă
50 min de citit Avansat Blocul fundamental de construcție al fiecărui LLM modern

Introducere: De la componente la un bloc complet

De-a lungul ultimelor lecții, am construit patru componente critice, una câte una:

  • Multi-Head Causal Self-Attention (Lecțiile 13-18) — permite fiecărui token să acorde atenție token-urilor anterioare prin mai multe capete de atenție paralele
  • Rețeaua Feed-Forward cu GELU (Lecția 19) — aplică o transformare neliniară independent la fiecare poziție de token
  • Layer Normalization (Lecția 20) — stabilizează antrenamentul prin normalizarea statisticilor de activare
  • Conexiuni Reziduale (Lecția 21) — creează autostrăzi informaționale care permit gradienților să circule prin rețele adânci

Fiecare dintre aceste componente, individual, rezolvă o problemă specifică. Dar magia arhitecturii Transformer constă în modul în care sunt combinate. În această lecție, le vom asambla în Blocul Transformer — unitatea unică, repetabilă care este stivuită pentru a crea GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, LLaMA și practic orice model de limbaj modern.

Perspectivă cheie: Un Bloc Transformer este ca o cărămidă LEGO. Fiecare cărămidă este identică ca structură. Dar stivuind multe dintre ele, poți construi orice, de la un perete simplu la un castel elaborat. Similar, GPT-2 Small stivuiește 12 Blocuri Transformer identice; GPT-3 stivuiește 96. Același design de bloc, repetat, produce capabilități emergente pe care niciun bloc individual nu le-ar putea atinge singur.

Arhitectura Blocului Transformer Pre-Norm

Există două variante principale ale Blocului Transformer, care diferă prin locul unde se aplică Layer Normalization:

  • Post-Norm (Transformer-ul original din 2017): Aplică LayerNorm după adunarea reziduală
  • Pre-Norm (GPT-2 și cele mai multe LLM-uri moderne): Aplică LayerNorm înainte de sub-stratul respectiv

Vom implementa varianta Pre-Norm, care este cea folosită de GPT-2 și care a devenit standardul în practica modernă. Pre-Norm este mai stabil în timpul antrenamentului deoarece calea reziduală rămâne „curată" — semnalul principal trece fără a fi distorsionat de normalizare.

Cele două sub-straturi

Un Bloc Transformer constă din exact două sub-straturi, fiecare încapsulat cu o conexiune reziduală:

Blocul Transformer (Pre-Norm)

Sub-stratul 1: Atenție

x = x + MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm(x))

Sub-stratul 2: Feed-Forward

x = x + FeedForward(LayerNorm(x))

Să urmărim exact ce se întâmplă pas cu pas:

  1. Intrarea x ajunge cu forma (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
  2. LayerNorm1(x) — normalizează pe dimensiunea d_model
  3. MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm1(x)) — calculează atenția; ieșirea are aceeași formă
  4. x = x + attention_output — conexiunea reziduală adaugă înapoi intrarea originală
  5. LayerNorm2(x) — normalizează din nou (folosind un LayerNorm diferit cu parametrii proprii)
  6. FeedForward(LayerNorm2(x)) — extinde la 4×d_model, aplică GELU, proiectează înapoi la d_model
  7. x = x + ffn_output — a doua conexiune reziduală
  8. Ieșirea x cu forma (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) — aceeași formă ca intrarea!
Analogie: Blocul Transformer ca un comitet de experți

Gândește-te la un Bloc Transformer ca la un proces de evaluare în două faze al unui comitet. În prima fază (atenția), fiecare membru al comitetului se uită la ce au spus toți ceilalți și adună contextul relevant. În a doua fază (feed-forward), fiecare membru procesează independent ce a învățat, aplicându-și propria expertiză profundă pentru a forma o opinie rafinată. Conexiunile reziduale sunt ca păstrarea notițelor tale originale — chiar și după ce ai ascultat de la alții și ai gândit profund, nu îți arunci înțelegerea inițială; adaugi la ea.

De ce contează această ordine specifică

Ordinea — mai întâi atenția, apoi feed-forward — nu este arbitrară. Există un motiv conceptual profund:

  • Atenția este un mecanism de comunicare. Permite token-urilor să partajeze informații între poziții. După atenție, reprezentarea fiecărui token este un amestec de informații de la el însuși și de la alte token-uri din secvență.
  • Feed-Forward este un mecanism de calcul. Procesează reprezentarea fiecărui token independent, aplicând transformări învățate. Preia informația amestecată din atenție și „reflectează" asupra ei.

Aceasta creează un tipar puternic: comunică, apoi calculează. Comunică, apoi calculează. Fiecare bloc rafinează reprezentările adunând mai întâi context și apoi procesându-l.

Perspectivă din cercetare: Cercetările Anthropic privind interpretabilitatea mecanistică au arătat că aceste două sub-straturi îndeplinesc funcții fundamental diferite. Capetele de atenție dezvoltă roluri specializate precum „capete de inducție" (potrivire de tipare) și „capete de poziție" (urmărirea pozițiilor relative), în timp ce straturile feed-forward acționează ca memorii cheie-valoare care stochează cunoștințe factuale. Combinația este ceea ce face Transformer-ele atât de puternice.

Asamblarea Blocului Transformer

Să implementăm acum un Bloc Transformer complet în NumPy. Vom include fiecare sub-componentă (pe care le-am construit în lecțiile anterioare) și le vom combina într-o singură clasă TransformerBlock curată. Observați cât de simplă este asamblarea — toată complexitatea este ascunsă în interiorul fiecărei componente:

Python

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# (Component classes defined as above)
class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-5):
 self.gamma = np.ones(d_model)
 self.beta = np.zeros(d_model)
 self.eps = eps
 def forward(self, x):
 mean = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 var = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.n_heads = n_heads
 self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
 scale = np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.W_q = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_k = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_v = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_o = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x @ self.W_q).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 K = (x @ self.W_k).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 V = (x @ self.W_v).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 scores = Q @ K.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2) / np.sqrt(self.head_dim)
 mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1) * (-1e9)
 scores = scores + mask
 exp_s = np.exp(scores - np.max(scores, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
 attn = exp_s / np.sum(exp_s, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 out = (attn @ V).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, T, C)
 return out @ self.W_o

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):
 d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d_model, d_ff) / np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(d_ff)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(d_ff, d_model) / np.sqrt(d_ff)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d_model)
 def gelu(self, x):
 return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x**3)))
 def forward(self, x):
 return self.gelu(x @ self.W1 + self.b1) @ self.W2 + self.b2

# ============================================================
# THE TRANSFORMER BLOCK - The core repeatable unit
# ============================================================
class TransformerBlock:
 """A single Transformer block using Pre-Norm architecture (GPT-2 style).

 Architecture:
 x -> LayerNorm -> MultiHeadAttention -> + (residual) ->
 -> LayerNorm -> FeedForward -> + (residual) -> output
 """
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before attention
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads) # Multi-head attention
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before FFN
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model) # Feed-forward network

 def forward(self, x):
 # Sub-layer 1: LayerNorm -> Attention -> Residual Add
 attn_output = self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + attn_output # Residual connection

 # Sub-layer 2: LayerNorm -> FFN -> Residual Add
 ffn_output = self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 x = x + ffn_output # Residual connection

 return x

Priviți! Forma intrării (2, 8, 64) este egală cu forma ieșirii (2, 8, 64). Aceasta este proprietatea critică ce permite stivuirea: fiecare Bloc Transformer primește un tensor de forma (batch, seq_len, d_model) și produce un tensor de exact aceeași formă. Aceasta înseamnă că putem înlănțui oricâte blocuri dorim, fiecare rafinând reprezentările mai departe.

Călătoria unui token prin bloc

Să urmărim ce se întâmplă cu un singur token (să zicem, la poziția 2) pe măsură ce trece prin Blocul Transformer:

  1. LayerNorm — Reprezentarea token-ului este normalizată la medie zero, varianță unitară
  2. Atenție — Token-ul acordă atenție pozițiilor [0, 1, 2] (masca cauzală blochează poziția 3+). Calculează o sumă ponderată a valorilor, adunând context din token-urile anterioare
  3. Adunare Reziduală — Reprezentarea originală este adăugată înapoi, păstrând ceea ce token-ul deja „știa"
  4. LayerNorm — Normalizează din nou cu un set separat de parametri
  5. FFN — Extinde la 4×d_model, aplică GELU, proiectează înapoi. Aceasta este „gândirea" independentă la fiecare poziție
  6. Adunare Reziduală — Din nou, adaugă înapoi reprezentarea de dinainte de FFN

După un bloc, reprezentarea token-ului conține: (a) informația sa originală, (b) informație contextuală de la alte token-uri și (c) transformări neliniare ale informației combinate. Semnificația sa a fost îmbogățită în timp ce identitatea sa este păstrată.

Analogie: Un student într-un grup de studiu

Gândește-te la un student (token-ul de la poziția 2) care studiază pentru un examen. Mai întâi, ascultă ce au de spus partenerii de studiu și evaluează contribuțiile după relevanță (atenție). Nu uită ce știa deja (adunare reziduală). Apoi reflectează profund și independent asupra a ceea ce a învățat (FFN), din nou fără a renunța la cunoștințele acumulate (adunare reziduală). După mai multe runde (blocuri stivuite), înțelegerea devine profundă și nuanțată.

Stivuirea blocurilor: Cum adâncimea creează capabilitate

Un singur Bloc Transformer poate face lucruri utile, dar puterea reală vine din stivuire. Iată ce știm despre modul în care adâncimea creează capabilități emergente:

1-2 blocuriPotrivire simplă de tipare, statistici de bigrame/trigrame"The cat sat on the ___" → "mat"
4-6 blocuriStructură sintactică, reguli gramaticale de bazăAcordul subiect-verb la distanță

Blocurile timpurii tind să învețe trăsături sintactice (gramatică, ordinea cuvintelor), blocurile de mijloc învață trăsături semantice (semnificație, relații), iar blocurile târzii învață trăsături specifice sarcinii (completarea prompturilor, răspunsul la întrebări). Acest lucru este similar cu modul în care straturile într-un CNN învață margini, apoi texturi, apoi obiecte.

Stivuirea mai multor blocuri

Să stivuim câteva Blocuri Transformer și să observăm cum evoluează reprezentările odată cu adâncimea:

# LN = LayerNorm, Attn = CausalSelfAttention, FFN = FeedForward, Bk = TransformerBlock
# These are functionally identical to the verbose versions from earlier lectures.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(d), np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 m = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 v = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - m) / np.sqrt(v + 1e-5)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.h, self.hd = h, d // h
 s = np.sqrt(d)
 self.Wq = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wk = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wv = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wo = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x@self.Wq).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 K = (x@self.Wk).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 V = (x@self.Wv).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 s = Q@K.transpose(0,1,3,2)/np.sqrt(self.hd)
 s = s + np.triu(np.ones((T,T)),k=1)*(-1e9)
 e = np.exp(s - np.max(s,axis=-1,keepdims=True))
 a = e / np.sum(e,axis=-1,keepdims=True)
 return (a@V).transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(B,T,C)@self.Wo

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d,4*d)/np.sqrt(d)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(4*d)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(4*d,d)/np.sqrt(4*d)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 h = x@self.W1+self.b1
 h = 0.5*h*(1+np.tanh(np.sqrt(2/np.pi)*(h+0.044715*h**3)))
 return h@self.W2+self.b2

class TransformerBlock:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d, h)
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 x = x + self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 return x

# Stack 6 Transformer Blocks

Numărul de parametri ai unui Bloc Transformer

Înțelegerea numărului de parametri este esențială pentru a aprecia scala modelului. Să numărăm fiecare parametru care poate fi învățat într-un singur Bloc Transformer:

Parametri într-un singur Bloc Transformer

LayerNorm 1: γ (d_model) + β (d_model) = 2 × d_model

Multi-Head Attention:

  • WQ: d_model × d_model
  • WK: d_model × d_model
  • WV: d_model × d_model
  • WO: d_model × d_model
  • Total: 4 × d_model2

LayerNorm 2: 2 × d_model

Rețea Feed-Forward:

  • W1: d_model × 4d_model
  • b1: 4d_model
  • W2: 4d_model × d_model
  • b2: d_model
  • Total: 8 × d_model2 + 5 × d_model

Total general per bloc: 12 × d_model2 + 9 × d_model

Pentru GPT-2 Small (d_model = 768): 12 × 7682 + 9 × 768 = 7.084.032 + 6.912 = ~7,09M parametri per bloc

Cu 12 blocuri: ~85M parametri (doar în Blocurile Transformer)

De ce funcționează atât de bine Blocul Transformer

Designul Blocului Transformer încorporează câteva principii cheie care îl fac remarcabil de eficient:

  1. Separarea responsabilităților: Atenția gestionează comunicarea între token-uri; FFN gestionează calculul per token. Acestea sunt operații fundamental diferite, iar menținerea lor separate permite fiecăreia să se specializeze.
  2. Flux grațios al gradienților: Conexiunile reziduale asigură că gradienții pot circula direct de la ieșire înapoi la intrare, chiar și prin 96+ straturi. Fără conexiuni reziduale, antrenarea unor rețele atât de adânci ar fi imposibilă.
  3. Dinamică stabilă de antrenament: LayerNorm Pre-Norm asigură că intrările pentru fiecare sub-strat au statistici bine comportate (medie zero, varianță unitară), prevenind activările extreme care ar destabiliza antrenamentul.
  4. Compozabilitate: Deoarece formele intrării și ieșirii se potrivesc, blocurile pot fi stivuite la nesfârșit. Aceasta este cheia scalării — mai multe blocuri înseamnă mai multă capacitate fără nicio modificare arhitecturală.
  5. Paralelism: Spre deosebire de RNN-uri, atenția pe întreaga secvență poate fi calculată în paralel. Acesta este motivul pentru care GPU-urile sunt atât de eficiente pentru antrenamentul Transformer.
Concepție greșită frecventă

Mulți oameni cred că trebuie să înțelegi Blocul Transformer ca un singur mecanism monolitic și complex. În realitate, este doar patru componente simple combinate într-un tipar specific. Dacă înțelegi LayerNorm, Attention, FFN și Conexiunile Reziduale individual, înțelegi Blocul Transformer. Nu există un „al cincilea ingredient" — magia este în combinație și repetare.

Rezumat

În această lecție, am asamblat Blocul Transformer — unitatea repetabilă fundamentală a fiecărui LLM modern. Am văzut cum:

  • Arhitectura Pre-Norm aplică LayerNorm înainte de fiecare sub-strat, menținând calea reziduală curată
  • Sub-stratul 1 (atenția) gestionează comunicarea între token-uri
  • Sub-stratul 2 (FFN) gestionează calculul în interiorul fiecărui token
  • Conexiunile reziduale păstrează informația și permit fluxul gradienților
  • Formele intrării și ieșirii sunt identice, permițând stivuirea arbitrară
  • Stivuirea creează capabilități emergente pe care niciun bloc individual nu le poate atinge

În lecția următoare, vom folosi aceste blocuri pentru a asambla arhitectura GPT completă — adăugând embedding-uri de token, embedding-uri poziționale și capul de proiecție de ieșire pentru a crea un model care poate procesa efectiv text și genera predicții.

Βασική ιδέα: Ένα Μπλοκ Transformer είναι σαν ένα τουβλάκι LEGO. Κάθε τουβλάκι είναι πανομοιότυπο σε δομή. Αλλά στοιβάζοντας πολλά από αυτά, μπορείς να χτίσεις οτιδήποτε, από έναν απλό τοίχο μέχρι ένα επιβλητικό κάστρο. Αντίστοιχα, το GPT-2 Small στοιβάζει 12 πανομοιότυπα Μπλοκ Transformer· το GPT-3 στοιβάζει 96. Ο ίδιος σχεδιασμός μπλοκ, επαναλαμβανόμενος, παράγει αναδυόμενες ικανότητες που κανένα μεμονωμένο μπλοκ δεν θα μπορούσε να επιτύχει μόνο του.

Η αρχιτεκτονική Pre-Norm του Μπλοκ Transformer

Υπάρχουν δύο κύριες παραλλαγές του Μπλοκ Transformer, που διαφέρουν στο πού εφαρμόζεται η Layer Normalization:

  • Post-Norm (ο αρχικός Transformer του 2017): Εφαρμόζει LayerNorm μετά την υπολειμματική πρόσθεση
  • Pre-Norm (GPT-2 και τα περισσότερα σύγχρονα LLM): Εφαρμόζει LayerNorm πριν από το υπο-επίπεδο

Θα υλοποιήσουμε την παραλλαγή Pre-Norm, που είναι αυτή που χρησιμοποιεί το GPT-2 και που έχει γίνει το πρότυπο στη σύγχρονη πρακτική. Η Pre-Norm είναι πιο σταθερή κατά τη διάρκεια της εκπαίδευσης επειδή η υπολειμματική διαδρομή παραμένει «καθαρή» — το κύριο σήμα περνά χωρίς να παραμορφώνεται από την κανονικοποίηση.

Τα δύο υπο-επίπεδα

Ένα Μπλοκ Transformer αποτελείται από ακριβώς δύο υπο-επίπεδα, καθένα τυλιγμένο με μια υπολειμματική σύνδεση:

Μπλοκ Transformer (Pre-Norm)

Υπο-επίπεδο 1: Προσοχή

x = x + MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm(x))

Υπο-επίπεδο 2: Feed-Forward

x = x + FeedForward(LayerNorm(x))

Ας παρακολουθήσουμε ακριβώς τι συμβαίνει βήμα προς βήμα:

  1. Η είσοδος x φτάνει με σχήμα (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
  2. LayerNorm1(x) — κανονικοποιεί κατά μήκος της διάστασης d_model
  3. MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm1(x)) — υπολογίζει την προσοχή· η έξοδος έχει το ίδιο σχήμα
  4. x = x + attention_output — η υπολειμματική σύνδεση προσθέτει πίσω την αρχική είσοδο
  5. LayerNorm2(x) — κανονικοποιεί ξανά (χρησιμοποιώντας ένα διαφορετικό LayerNorm με τις δικές του παραμέτρους)
  6. FeedForward(LayerNorm2(x)) — επεκτείνει σε 4×d_model, εφαρμόζει GELU, προβάλλει πίσω σε d_model
  7. x = x + ffn_output — δεύτερη υπολειμματική σύνδεση
  8. Η έξοδος x με σχήμα (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) — ίδιο σχήμα με την είσοδο!
Αναλογία: Το Μπλοκ Transformer ως επιτροπή ειδικών

Σκεφτείτε ένα Μπλοκ Transformer ως μια διαδικασία αξιολόγησης δύο φάσεων από μια επιτροπή. Στην πρώτη φάση (προσοχή), κάθε μέλος της επιτροπής εξετάζει τι έχουν πει όλοι οι άλλοι και συγκεντρώνει το σχετικό πλαίσιο. Στη δεύτερη φάση (feed-forward), κάθε μέλος επεξεργάζεται ανεξάρτητα αυτά που έμαθε, εφαρμόζοντας τη δική του βαθιά εμπειρογνωμοσύνη για να σχηματίσει μια εκλεπτυσμένη γνώμη. Οι υπολειμματικές συνδέσεις είναι σαν να κρατάτε τις αρχικές σας σημειώσεις — ακόμα και αφού ακούσετε τους άλλους και σκεφτείτε βαθιά, δεν απορρίπτετε την αρχική σας κατανόηση· προσθέτετε σε αυτήν.

Γιατί αυτή η συγκεκριμένη σειρά έχει σημασία

Η σειρά — πρώτα η προσοχή, μετά το feed-forward — δεν είναι αυθαίρετη. Υπάρχει ένας βαθύς εννοιολογικός λόγος:

  • Η προσοχή είναι ένας μηχανισμός επικοινωνίας. Επιτρέπει στα tokens να μοιράζονται πληροφορίες μεταξύ θέσεων. Μετά την προσοχή, η αναπαράσταση κάθε token είναι ένα μίγμα πληροφοριών από τον εαυτό του και άλλα tokens στην ακολουθία.
  • Το Feed-Forward είναι ένας μηχανισμός υπολογισμού. Επεξεργάζεται την αναπαράσταση κάθε token ανεξάρτητα, εφαρμόζοντας μαθημένους μετασχηματισμούς. Παίρνει τις μικτές πληροφορίες από την προσοχή και «σκέφτεται» πάνω σε αυτές.

Αυτό δημιουργεί ένα ισχυρό μοτίβο: επικοινώνησε, μετά υπολόγισε. Επικοινώνησε, μετά υπολόγισε. Κάθε μπλοκ βελτιώνει τις αναπαραστάσεις συγκεντρώνοντας πρώτα πλαίσιο και μετά επεξεργάζοντάς το.

Ερευνητική προοπτική: Η έρευνα της Anthropic στη μηχανιστική ερμηνευσιμότητα έχει δείξει ότι αυτά τα δύο υπο-επίπεδα εκτελούν θεμελιωδώς διαφορετικές λειτουργίες. Οι κεφαλές προσοχής αναπτύσσουν εξειδικευμένους ρόλους όπως «κεφαλές επαγωγής» (αντιστοίχιση μοτίβων) και «κεφαλές θέσης» (παρακολούθηση σχετικών θέσεων), ενώ τα επίπεδα feed-forward λειτουργούν ως μνήμες κλειδιού-τιμής που αποθηκεύουν πραγματική γνώση. Ο συνδυασμός είναι αυτό που κάνει τα Transformers τόσο ισχυρά.

Συναρμολόγηση του Μπλοκ Transformer

Ας υλοποιήσουμε τώρα ένα πλήρες Μπλοκ Transformer σε NumPy. Θα συμπεριλάβουμε κάθε υπο-στοιχείο (που κατασκευάσαμε σε προηγούμενες διαλέξεις) και θα τα συνδυάσουμε σε μια ενιαία, καθαρή κλάση TransformerBlock. Παρατηρήστε πόσο απλή είναι η συναρμολόγηση — όλη η πολυπλοκότητα είναι κρυμμένη μέσα σε κάθε στοιχείο:

Python

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# (Component classes defined as above)
class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-5):
 self.gamma = np.ones(d_model)
 self.beta = np.zeros(d_model)
 self.eps = eps
 def forward(self, x):
 mean = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 var = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.n_heads = n_heads
 self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
 scale = np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.W_q = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_k = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_v = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_o = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x @ self.W_q).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 K = (x @ self.W_k).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 V = (x @ self.W_v).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 scores = Q @ K.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2) / np.sqrt(self.head_dim)
 mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1) * (-1e9)
 scores = scores + mask
 exp_s = np.exp(scores - np.max(scores, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
 attn = exp_s / np.sum(exp_s, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 out = (attn @ V).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, T, C)
 return out @ self.W_o

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):
 d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d_model, d_ff) / np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(d_ff)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(d_ff, d_model) / np.sqrt(d_ff)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d_model)
 def gelu(self, x):
 return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x**3)))
 def forward(self, x):
 return self.gelu(x @ self.W1 + self.b1) @ self.W2 + self.b2

# ============================================================
# THE TRANSFORMER BLOCK - The core repeatable unit
# ============================================================
class TransformerBlock:
 """A single Transformer block using Pre-Norm architecture (GPT-2 style).

 Architecture:
 x -> LayerNorm -> MultiHeadAttention -> + (residual) ->
 -> LayerNorm -> FeedForward -> + (residual) -> output
 """
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before attention
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads) # Multi-head attention
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before FFN
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model) # Feed-forward network

 def forward(self, x):
 # Sub-layer 1: LayerNorm -> Attention -> Residual Add
 attn_output = self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + attn_output # Residual connection

 # Sub-layer 2: LayerNorm -> FFN -> Residual Add
 ffn_output = self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 x = x + ffn_output # Residual connection

 return x

# Test the Transformer Block
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
batch_size = 2
seq_len = 8

block = TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads)
x = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, d_model)

print(f"Transformer Block Configuration:")
print(f" d_model = {d_model}")
print(f" n_heads = {n_heads}")
print(f" head_dim = {d_model // n_heads}")
print(f" d_ff = {4 * d_model}")
print()

print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
output = block.forward(x)
print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
print(f"Shape preserved: {x.shape == output.shape}")
print()

# Verify the output is different from input (the block did something!)
diff = np.mean(np.abs(output - x))
print(f"Mean absolute change: {diff:.6f}")
print(f"This confirms the block is processing the data, not just passing it through.")

Κοιτάξτε! Το σχήμα εισόδου (2, 8, 64) ισούται με το σχήμα εξόδου (2, 8, 64). Αυτή είναι η κρίσιμη ιδιότητα που επιτρέπει τη στοίβαξη: κάθε Μπλοκ Transformer δέχεται έναν τανυστή σχήματος (batch, seq_len, d_model) και παράγει έναν τανυστή ακριβώς ίδιου σχήματος. Αυτό σημαίνει ότι μπορούμε να αλυσοδέσουμε όσα μπλοκ θέλουμε, καθένα βελτιώνοντας περαιτέρω τις αναπαραστάσεις.

Το ταξίδι ενός token μέσα από το μπλοκ

Ας παρακολουθήσουμε τι συμβαίνει σε ένα μεμονωμένο token (π.χ. στη θέση 2) καθώς περνά μέσα από το Μπλοκ Transformer:

  1. LayerNorm — Η αναπαράσταση του token κανονικοποιείται σε μηδενικό μέσο όρο, μοναδιαία διακύμανση
  2. Προσοχή — Το token δίνει προσοχή στις θέσεις [0, 1, 2] (η αιτιακή μάσκα αποκλείει τη θέση 3+). Υπολογίζει ένα σταθμισμένο άθροισμα τιμών, συγκεντρώνοντας πλαίσιο από προηγούμενα tokens
  3. Υπολειμματική πρόσθεση — Η αρχική αναπαράσταση προστίθεται πίσω, διατηρώντας αυτό που το token ήδη «γνώριζε»
  4. LayerNorm — Κανονικοποίηση ξανά με ένα ξεχωριστό σύνολο παραμέτρων
  5. FFN — Επέκταση σε 4×d_model, εφαρμογή GELU, προβολή πίσω. Αυτή είναι η ανεξάρτητη «σκέψη» σε κάθε θέση
  6. Υπολειμματική πρόσθεση — Και πάλι, προσθέτει πίσω την αναπαράσταση από πριν το FFN

Μετά από ένα μπλοκ, η αναπαράσταση του token περιέχει: (α) τις αρχικές του πληροφορίες, (β) πληροφορίες πλαισίου από άλλα tokens, και (γ) μη γραμμικούς μετασχηματισμούς των συνδυασμένων πληροφοριών. Η σημασία του έχει εμπλουτιστεί ενώ η ταυτότητά του διατηρείται.

Αναλογία: Ένας φοιτητής σε ομάδα μελέτης

Σκεφτείτε έναν φοιτητή (token στη θέση 2) που διαβάζει για εξετάσεις. Πρώτα, ακούει τι έχουν να πουν οι συνάδελφοι μελέτης και σταθμίζει τις συνεισφορές ανάλογα με τη σχετικότητα (προσοχή). Δεν ξεχνά αυτά που ήδη γνώριζε (υπολειμματική πρόσθεση). Στη συνέχεια, σκέφτεται βαθιά και ανεξάρτητα γι' αυτά που έμαθε (FFN), και πάλι χωρίς να απορρίψει τη συσσωρευμένη γνώση (υπολειμματική πρόσθεση). Μετά από πολλαπλούς γύρους (στοιβαγμένα μπλοκ), η κατανόηση γίνεται βαθιά και λεπτή.

Στοίβαξη μπλοκ: Πώς το βάθος δημιουργεί ικανότητα

Ένα μεμονωμένο Μπλοκ Transformer μπορεί να κάνει χρήσιμη δουλειά, αλλά η πραγματική δύναμη προέρχεται από τη στοίβαξη. Να τι γνωρίζουμε σχετικά με τον τρόπο που το βάθος δημιουργεί αναδυόμενες ικανότητες:

ΒάθοςΤι μπορεί να μάθει το μοντέλοΠαράδειγμα
1-2 μπλοκΑπλή αντιστοίχιση μοτίβων, στατιστικά bigram/trigram"The cat sat on the ___" → "mat"
4-6 μπλοκΣυντακτική δομή, βασικοί γραμματικοί κανόνεςΣυμφωνία υποκειμένου-ρήματος σε απόσταση
8-12 μπλοκΣημασιολογική κατανόηση, ανάκληση πραγματικών δεδομένων"The capital of France is ___" → "Paris"
24-48 μπλοκΣύνθετη συλλογιστική, μάθηση εντός πλαισίουΑκολουθώντας οδηγίες, μάθηση few-shot
96+ μπλοκΑναδυόμενες ικανότητες: αλυσίδα σκέψης, αναλογική συλλογιστικήΜαθηματικά πολλαπλών βημάτων, δημιουργία κώδικα
Βασική ιδέα: Κάθε μπλοκ δεν χρειάζεται να μάθει τα πάντα. Τα πρώτα μπλοκ τείνουν να μαθαίνουν συντακτικά χαρακτηριστικά (γραμματική, σειρά λέξεων), τα μεσαία μπλοκ μαθαίνουν σημασιολογικά χαρακτηριστικά (νόημα, σχέσεις) και τα τελευταία μπλοκ μαθαίνουν χαρακτηριστικά συγκεκριμένα για κάθε εργασία (συμπλήρωση prompts, απάντηση ερωτήσεων). Αυτό μοιάζει με τον τρόπο που τα επίπεδα σε ένα CNN μαθαίνουν ακμές, μετά υφές, μετά αντικείμενα.

Στοίβαξη πολλαπλών μπλοκ

Ας στοιβάξουμε αρκετά Μπλοκ Transformer και ας παρατηρήσουμε πώς εξελίσσονται οι αναπαραστάσεις με το βάθος:

Python

# Compact class names used from here onward:
# LN = LayerNorm, Attn = CausalSelfAttention, FFN = FeedForward, Bk = TransformerBlock
# These are functionally identical to the verbose versions from earlier lectures.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(d), np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 m = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 v = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - m) / np.sqrt(v + 1e-5)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.h, self.hd = h, d // h
 s = np.sqrt(d)
 self.Wq = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wk = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wv = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wo = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x@self.Wq).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 K = (x@self.Wk).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 V = (x@self.Wv).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 s = Q@K.transpose(0,1,3,2)/np.sqrt(self.hd)
 s = s + np.triu(np.ones((T,T)),k=1)*(-1e9)
 e = np.exp(s - np.max(s,axis=-1,keepdims=True))
 a = e / np.sum(e,axis=-1,keepdims=True)
 return (a@V).transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(B,T,C)@self.Wo

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d,4*d)/np.sqrt(d)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(4*d)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(4*d,d)/np.sqrt(4*d)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 h = x@self.W1+self.b1
 h = 0.5*h*(1+np.tanh(np.sqrt(2/np.pi)*(h+0.044715*h**3)))
 return h@self.W2+self.b2

class TransformerBlock:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d, h)
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 x = x + self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 return x

# Stack 6 Transformer Blocks
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
n_layers = 6

blocks = [TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads) for _ in range(n_layers)]

# Input
x = np.random.randn(1, 8, d_model) * 0.02 # Small initial values (like embeddings)

print("=== Passing Data Through 6 Stacked Transformer Blocks ===")
print(f"Config: d_model={d_model}, n_heads={n_heads}, n_layers={n_layers}")
print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
print()

# Track statistics at each layer
initial_repr = x[0, 0].copy() # Track first token

for i, block in enumerate(blocks):
 x = block.forward(x)
 token_repr = x[0, 0]

 # How different is this token's repr from the original?
 cosine_sim = np.dot(initial_repr, token_repr) / (
 np.linalg.norm(initial_repr) * np.linalg.norm(token_repr) + 1e-10
 )

 print(f"After Block {i+1}:")
 print(f" Output shape: {x.shape}")
 print(f" Mean: {np.mean(x):.6f} Std: {np.std(x):.4f}")
 print(f" Cosine similarity to input: {cosine_sim:.4f}")
 print()

print("Key Observations:")
print(" 1. Shape is preserved through ALL blocks (required for stacking)")
print(" 2. The representation evolves - cosine similarity to input changes")
print(" 3. Each block transforms the representation, building on previous blocks")
print(" 4. This is exactly how GPT-2 processes text through 12 blocks")

Αριθμός παραμέτρων ενός Μπλοκ Transformer

Η κατανόηση του αριθμού παραμέτρων είναι απαραίτητη για να εκτιμήσουμε την κλίμακα του μοντέλου. Ας μετρήσουμε κάθε εκπαιδεύσιμη παράμετρο σε ένα μεμονωμένο Μπλοκ Transformer:

Παράμετροι σε ένα Μπλοκ Transformer

LayerNorm 1: γ (d_model) + β (d_model) = 2 × d_model

Multi-Head Attention:

  • WQ: d_model × d_model
  • WK: d_model × d_model
  • WV: d_model × d_model
  • WO: d_model × d_model
  • Σύνολο: 4 × d_model2

LayerNorm 2: 2 × d_model

Δίκτυο Feed-Forward:

  • W1: d_model × 4d_model
  • b1: 4d_model
  • W2: 4d_model × d_model
  • b2: d_model
  • Σύνολο: 8 × d_model2 + 5 × d_model

Γενικό σύνολο ανά μπλοκ: 12 × d_model2 + 9 × d_model

Για GPT-2 Small (d_model = 768): 12 × 7682 + 9 × 768 = 7.084.032 + 6.912 = ~7,09M παράμετροι ανά μπλοκ

Με 12 μπλοκ: ~85M παράμετροι (μόνο στα Μπλοκ Transformer)

Γιατί το Μπλοκ Transformer λειτουργεί τόσο καλά

Ο σχεδιασμός του Μπλοκ Transformer ενσωματώνει αρκετές βασικές αρχές που το καθιστούν εξαιρετικά αποτελεσματικό:

  1. Διαχωρισμός ευθυνών: Η προσοχή χειρίζεται τη διά-token επικοινωνία· το FFN χειρίζεται τον υπολογισμό ανά token. Αυτές είναι θεμελιωδώς διαφορετικές λειτουργίες, και η διατήρησή τους ξεχωριστά επιτρέπει στην καθεμία να εξειδικευτεί.
  2. Ομαλή ροή κλίσεων: Οι υπολειμματικές συνδέσεις εξασφαλίζουν ότι οι κλίσεις μπορούν να ρεύσουν απευθείας από την έξοδο πίσω στην είσοδο, ακόμα και μέσα από 96+ επίπεδα. Χωρίς υπολειμματικές συνδέσεις, η εκπαίδευση τόσο βαθιών δικτύων θα ήταν αδύνατη.
  3. Σταθερή δυναμική εκπαίδευσης: Η Pre-Norm LayerNorm εξασφαλίζει ότι οι είσοδοι σε κάθε υπο-επίπεδο έχουν καλοσυμπεριφερόμενα στατιστικά (μηδενικός μέσος, μοναδιαία διακύμανση), αποτρέποντας τις ακραίες ενεργοποιήσεις που θα αποσταθεροποιούσαν την εκπαίδευση.
  4. Συνθεσιμότητα: Επειδή τα σχήματα εισόδου και εξόδου ταιριάζουν, τα μπλοκ μπορούν να στοιβαχτούν επ' αόριστον. Αυτό είναι το κλειδί της κλιμάκωσης — περισσότερα μπλοκ σημαίνει μεγαλύτερη χωρητικότητα χωρίς αρχιτεκτονικές αλλαγές.
  5. Παραλληλισμός: Σε αντίθεση με τα RNN, η προσοχή σε ολόκληρη την ακολουθία μπορεί να υπολογιστεί παράλληλα. Αυτός είναι ο λόγος που οι GPU είναι τόσο αποτελεσματικές για την εκπαίδευση Transformer.
Συνηθισμένη παρανόηση

Πολλοί άνθρωποι πιστεύουν ότι πρέπει να κατανοήσεις το Μπλοκ Transformer ως έναν μονολιθικό, πολύπλοκο μηχανισμό. Στην πραγματικότητα, είναι απλώς τέσσερα απλά στοιχεία συνδυασμένα σε ένα συγκεκριμένο μοτίβο. Αν κατανοείς τα LayerNorm, Attention, FFN και τις Υπολειμματικές Συνδέσεις μεμονωμένα, κατανοείς το Μπλοκ Transformer. Δεν υπάρχει «πέμπτο συστατικό» — η μαγεία βρίσκεται στον συνδυασμό και την επανάληψη.

LECTURE 22 Stufe 4: Architektur

Der Transformer-Block

Multi-Head Attention, Feed-Forward-Netzwerke, Layer Normalization und Residual-Verbindungen zu einer einzigen, wiederholbaren Einheit kombinieren
50 Min. Lesezeit Fortgeschritten Der fundamentale Baustein jedes modernen LLM

Einführung: Von Komponenten zu einem vollständigen Block

In den letzten Vorlesungen haben wir vier kritische Komponenten Schritt für Schritt aufgebaut:

  • Multi-Head Causal Self-Attention (Vorlesungen 13-18) — ermöglicht es jedem Token, über mehrere parallele Attention-Köpfe auf vorherige Token zu achten
  • Feed-Forward-Netzwerk mit GELU (Vorlesung 19) — wendet unabhängig für jede Token-Position eine nichtlineare Transformation an
  • Layer Normalization (Vorlesung 20) — stabilisiert das Training durch Normalisierung der Aktivierungsstatistiken
  • Residual-Verbindungen (Vorlesung 21) — schaffen Informationsautobahnen, die es Gradienten erlauben, durch tiefe Netzwerke zu fließen

Jede dieser Komponenten löst für sich genommen ein spezifisches Problem. Die Magie der Transformer-Architektur liegt jedoch darin, wie sie kombiniert werden. In dieser Vorlesung setzen wir sie zum Transformer-Block zusammen — der einzelnen, wiederholbaren Einheit, die gestapelt wird, um GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, LLaMA und praktisch jedes moderne Sprachmodell zu erschaffen.

Kernidee: Ein Transformer-Block ist wie ein LEGO-Stein. Jeder Stein ist strukturell identisch. Aber indem man viele davon stapelt, kann man alles bauen, von einer einfachen Mauer bis zu einem prächtigen Schloss. Ähnlich stapelt GPT-2 Small 12 identische Transformer-Blöcke; GPT-3 stapelt 96. Das gleiche Blockdesign, wiederholt angewendet, erzeugt emergente Fähigkeiten, die kein einzelner Block allein erreichen könnte.

Die Pre-Norm-Transformer-Block-Architektur

Es gibt zwei Hauptvarianten des Transformer-Blocks, die sich darin unterscheiden, wo Layer Normalization angewendet wird:

  • Post-Norm (ursprünglicher Transformer von 2017): LayerNorm wird nach der Residual-Addition angewendet
  • Pre-Norm (GPT-2 und die meisten modernen LLMs): LayerNorm wird vor dem Sub-Layer angewendet

Wir werden die Pre-Norm-Variante implementieren, die GPT-2 verwendet und die zum Standard in der modernen Praxis geworden ist. Pre-Norm ist während des Trainings stabiler, weil der Residual-Pfad "sauber" bleibt — das Hauptsignal läuft durch, ohne durch Normalisierung verzerrt zu werden.

Die zwei Sub-Layer

Ein Transformer-Block besteht aus genau zwei Sub-Layern, von denen jeder mit einer Residual-Verbindung umschlossen ist:

Transformer-Block (Pre-Norm)

Sub-Layer 1: Attention

x = x + MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm(x))

Sub-Layer 2: Feed-Forward

x = x + FeedForward(LayerNorm(x))

Verfolgen wir Schritt für Schritt, was genau passiert:

  1. Eingabe x kommt mit der Form (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) an
  2. LayerNorm1(x) — normalisiert entlang der d_model-Dimension
  3. MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm1(x)) — berechnet Attention; die Ausgabe hat dieselbe Form
  4. x = x + attention_output — die Residual-Verbindung addiert die ursprüngliche Eingabe wieder hinzu
  5. LayerNorm2(x) — erneut normalisieren (mit einem anderen LayerNorm mit eigenen Parametern)
  6. FeedForward(LayerNorm2(x)) — auf 4×d_model erweitern, GELU anwenden, zurück auf d_model projizieren
  7. x = x + ffn_output — zweite Residual-Verbindung
  8. Ausgabe x mit der Form (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) — dieselbe Form wie die Eingabe!
Analogie: Der Transformer-Block als Expertengremium

Stellen Sie sich einen Transformer-Block als einen zweiphasigen Prüfungsprozess eines Gremiums vor. In der ersten Phase (Attention) betrachtet jedes Gremiumsmitglied, was alle anderen gesagt haben, und sammelt relevanten Kontext. In der zweiten Phase (Feed-Forward) verarbeitet jedes Mitglied unabhängig das Gelernte und wendet seine eigene tiefgehende Expertise an, um eine ausgereifte Meinung zu bilden. Die Residual-Verbindungen sind wie das Bewahren der eigenen Notizen — auch nachdem man andere angehört und gründlich nachgedacht hat, verwirft man sein ursprüngliches Verständnis nicht; man fügt ihm etwas hinzu.

Warum diese bestimmte Reihenfolge wichtig ist

Die Reihenfolge — zuerst Attention, dann Feed-Forward — ist nicht willkürlich. Es gibt dafür einen tiefen konzeptionellen Grund:

  • Attention ist ein Kommunikationsmechanismus. Er ermöglicht es Token, Informationen über Positionen hinweg zu teilen. Nach der Attention ist die Repräsentation jedes Tokens eine Mischung aus Informationen von sich selbst und von anderen Token in der Sequenz.
  • Feed-Forward ist ein Berechnungsmechanismus. Er verarbeitet die Repräsentation jedes Tokens unabhängig und wendet erlernte Transformationen an. Er nimmt die gemischten Informationen aus der Attention und "denkt darüber nach".

Das erzeugt ein mächtiges Muster: kommunizieren, dann berechnen. Kommunizieren, dann berechnen. Jeder Block verfeinert die Repräsentationen, indem er zunächst Kontext sammelt und ihn dann verarbeitet.

Forschungsperspektive: Anthropics Forschung zur mechanistischen Interpretierbarkeit hat gezeigt, dass diese beiden Sub-Layer grundlegend unterschiedliche Funktionen erfüllen. Attention-Köpfe entwickeln spezialisierte Rollen wie "Induction Heads" (Mustererkennung) und "Position Heads" (Verfolgung relativer Positionen), während Feed-Forward-Schichten als Key-Value-Speicher fungieren, die faktisches Wissen speichern. Die Kombination ist es, was Transformer so leistungsfähig macht.

Zusammensetzen des Transformer-Blocks

Implementieren wir nun einen vollständigen Transformer-Block in NumPy. Wir binden jede Teilkomponente ein (die wir in vorherigen Vorlesungen gebaut haben) und kombinieren sie zu einer einzigen, sauberen TransformerBlock-Klasse. Beachten Sie, wie einfach die Zusammensetzung ist — die gesamte Komplexität ist in jeder Komponente verborgen:

Python

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# (Component classes defined as above)
class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d_model, eps=1e-5):
 self.gamma = np.ones(d_model)
 self.beta = np.zeros(d_model)
 self.eps = eps
 def forward(self, x):
 mean = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 var = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.n_heads = n_heads
 self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
 scale = np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.W_q = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_k = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_v = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 self.W_o = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) / scale
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x @ self.W_q).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 K = (x @ self.W_k).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 V = (x @ self.W_v).reshape(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
 scores = Q @ K.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2) / np.sqrt(self.head_dim)
 mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1) * (-1e9)
 scores = scores + mask
 exp_s = np.exp(scores - np.max(scores, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
 attn = exp_s / np.sum(exp_s, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 out = (attn @ V).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, T, C)
 return out @ self.W_o

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):
 d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d_model, d_ff) / np.sqrt(d_model)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(d_ff)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(d_ff, d_model) / np.sqrt(d_ff)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d_model)
 def gelu(self, x):
 return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x**3)))
 def forward(self, x):
 return self.gelu(x @ self.W1 + self.b1) @ self.W2 + self.b2

# ============================================================
# THE TRANSFORMER BLOCK - The core repeatable unit
# ============================================================
class TransformerBlock:
 """A single Transformer block using Pre-Norm architecture (GPT-2 style).

 Architecture:
 x -> LayerNorm -> MultiHeadAttention -> + (residual) ->
 -> LayerNorm -> FeedForward -> + (residual) -> output
 """
 def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before attention
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads) # Multi-head attention
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d_model) # LayerNorm before FFN
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model) # Feed-forward network

 def forward(self, x):
 # Sub-layer 1: LayerNorm -> Attention -> Residual Add
 attn_output = self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + attn_output # Residual connection

 # Sub-layer 2: LayerNorm -> FFN -> Residual Add
 ffn_output = self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 x = x + ffn_output # Residual connection

 return x

# Test the Transformer Block
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
batch_size = 2
seq_len = 8

block = TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads)

print(f"Transformer Block Configuration:")
print(f" d_model = {d_model}")
print(f" n_heads = {n_heads}")
print(f" head_dim = {d_model // n_heads}")
print(f" d_ff = {4 * d_model}")
print()

print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
output = block.forward(x)
print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
print(f"Shape preserved: {x.shape == output.shape}")
print()

# Verify the output is different from input (the block did something!)
diff = np.mean(np.abs(output - x))
print(f"Mean absolute change: {diff:.6f}")

Sehen Sie sich das an! Die Eingabeform (2, 8, 64) entspricht der Ausgabeform (2, 8, 64). Dies ist die entscheidende Eigenschaft, die das Stapeln ermöglicht: jeder Transformer-Block nimmt einen Tensor der Form (batch, seq_len, d_model) entgegen und gibt einen Tensor mit exakt derselben Form aus. Das bedeutet, wir können so viele Blöcke aneinanderreihen, wie wir wollen, wobei jeder die Repräsentationen weiter verfeinert.

Die Reise eines Tokens durch den Block

Verfolgen wir, was mit einem einzelnen Token (sagen wir, an Position 2) geschieht, während es den Transformer-Block durchläuft:

  1. LayerNorm — Die Repräsentation des Tokens wird auf Mittelwert null und Einheitsvarianz normalisiert
  2. Attention — Das Token achtet auf die Positionen [0, 1, 2] (die kausale Maske blockiert Position 3+). Es berechnet eine gewichtete Summe der Values und sammelt so Kontext aus früheren Token
  3. Residual-Addition — Die ursprüngliche Repräsentation wird wieder hinzuaddiert und bewahrt so, was das Token bereits "wusste"
  4. LayerNorm — Erneut normalisieren, mit einem separaten Satz von Parametern
  5. FFN — Auf 4×d_model erweitern, GELU anwenden, zurückprojizieren. Dies ist unabhängiges "Denken" an jeder Position
  6. Residual-Addition — Erneut wird die Repräsentation von vor der FFN wieder hinzugefügt

Nach einem Block enthält die Repräsentation des Tokens: (a) seine ursprünglichen Informationen, (b) kontextuelle Informationen von anderen Token und (c) nichtlineare Transformationen der kombinierten Informationen. Seine Bedeutung wurde angereichert, während seine Identität erhalten bleibt.

Analogie: Ein Student in einer Lerngruppe

Stellen Sie sich einen Studenten (Token an Position 2) vor, der für eine Prüfung lernt. Zunächst hört er zu, was seine Lernpartner zu sagen haben, und gewichtet die Beiträge nach Relevanz (Attention). Er vergisst nicht, was er bereits wusste (Residual-Addition). Dann denkt er tief und eigenständig über das Gelernte nach (FFN), wiederum ohne das angesammelte Wissen zu verwerfen (Residual-Addition). Nach mehreren Runden (gestapelten Blöcken) wird das Verständnis tief und nuanciert.

Blöcke stapeln: Wie Tiefe Fähigkeiten schafft

Ein einzelner Transformer-Block kann nützliche Arbeit leisten, aber die eigentliche Kraft entsteht durch Stapeln. Hier ist, was wir darüber wissen, wie Tiefe emergente Fähigkeiten erzeugt:

Mehrere Blöcke stapeln

Stapeln wir mehrere Transformer-Blöcke und beobachten, wie sich die Repräsentationen mit der Tiefe entwickeln:

# Compact class names used from here onward:
# LN = LayerNorm, Attn = CausalSelfAttention, FFN = FeedForward, Bk = TransformerBlock
# These are functionally identical to the verbose versions from earlier lectures.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

class LayerNorm:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(d), np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 m = np.mean(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 v = np.var(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 return self.gamma * ((x - m) / np.sqrt(v + 1e-5)) + self.beta

class MultiHeadAttention:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.h, self.hd = h, d // h
 s = np.sqrt(d)
 self.Wq = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wk = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wv = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 self.Wo = np.random.randn(d, d)/s
 def forward(self, x):
 B, T, C = x.shape
 Q = (x@self.Wq).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 K = (x@self.Wk).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 V = (x@self.Wv).reshape(B,T,self.h,self.hd).transpose(0,2,1,3)
 s = Q@K.transpose(0,1,3,2)/np.sqrt(self.hd)
 s = s + np.triu(np.ones((T,T)),k=1)*(-1e9)
 e = np.exp(s - np.max(s,axis=-1,keepdims=True))
 a = e / np.sum(e,axis=-1,keepdims=True)
 return (a@V).transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(B,T,C)@self.Wo

class FeedForward:
 def __init__(self, d):
 self.W1 = np.random.randn(d,4*d)/np.sqrt(d)
 self.b1 = np.zeros(4*d)
 self.W2 = np.random.randn(4*d,d)/np.sqrt(4*d)
 self.b2 = np.zeros(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 h = x@self.W1+self.b1
 h = 0.5*h*(1+np.tanh(np.sqrt(2/np.pi)*(h+0.044715*h**3)))
 return h@self.W2+self.b2

class TransformerBlock:
 def __init__(self, d, h):
 self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d, h)
 self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d)
 self.ffn = FeedForward(d)
 def forward(self, x):
 x = x + self.attn.forward(self.ln1.forward(x))
 x = x + self.ffn.forward(self.ln2.forward(x))
 return x

# Stack 6 Transformer Blocks
d_model = 64
n_heads = 4
n_layers = 6

blocks = [TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads) for _ in range(n_layers)]

print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")

for i, block in enumerate(blocks):

 )

 print(f" Cosine similarity to input: {cosine_sim:.4f}")

print("Key Observations:")
print(" 1. Shape is preserved through ALL blocks (required for stacking)")
print(" 2. The representation evolves - cosine similarity to input changes")
print(" 3. Each block transforms the representation, building on previous blocks")

Parameteranzahl eines Transformer-Blocks

Das Verständnis der Parameteranzahl ist wesentlich, um die Modellgröße einordnen zu können. Zählen wir jeden lernbaren Parameter in einem einzelnen Transformer-Block:

LayerNorm 1: γ (d_model) + β (d_model) = 2 × d_model

  • WQ: d_model × d_model
  • WK: d_model × d_model
  • WV: d_model × d_model
  • WO: d_model × d_model

Warum der Transformer-Block so gut funktioniert

Das Design des Transformer-Blocks verkörpert mehrere Kernprinzipien, die ihn bemerkenswert effektiv machen:

  1. Trennung der Zuständigkeiten: Attention übernimmt die Kommunikation zwischen Token; FFN übernimmt die Berechnung pro Token. Dies sind grundlegend unterschiedliche Operationen, und die Trennung ermöglicht es jeder, sich zu spezialisieren.
  2. Reibungsloser Gradientenfluss: Die Residual-Verbindungen stellen sicher, dass Gradienten direkt von der Ausgabe zurück zur Eingabe fließen können, selbst durch 96+ Schichten. Ohne Residuen wäre das Training so tiefer Netzwerke unmöglich.
  3. Stabile Trainingsdynamik: Pre-Norm-LayerNorm stellt sicher, dass die Eingaben in jeden Sub-Layer wohlverhaltene Statistiken aufweisen (Mittelwert null, Einheitsvarianz), was die extremen Aktivierungen verhindert, die das Training destabilisieren würden.
  4. Kombinierbarkeit: Da Eingabe- und Ausgabeform übereinstimmen, können Blöcke beliebig gestapelt werden. Das ist der Schlüssel zur Skalierung — mehr Blöcke bedeuten mehr Kapazität, ohne architektonische Änderungen.
  5. Parallelität: Anders als bei RNNs kann Attention über die gesamte Sequenz parallel berechnet werden. Das macht GPUs für das Training von Transformern so effektiv.
Verbreitetes Missverständnis

Viele Menschen denken, man müsse den Transformer-Block als einen einzigen, monolithischen, komplexen Mechanismus verstehen. In Wirklichkeit sind es nur vier einfache Komponenten, die in einem bestimmten Muster kombiniert werden. Wenn Sie LayerNorm, Attention, FFN und Residual-Verbindungen einzeln verstehen, verstehen Sie den Transformer-Block. Es gibt keine "fünfte Zutat" — die Magie liegt in der Kombination und Wiederholung.

Zusammenfassung

In dieser Vorlesung haben wir den Transformer-Block zusammengesetzt — die fundamentale, wiederholbare Einheit jedes modernen LLM. Wir haben gesehen, wie:

  • Die Pre-Norm-Architektur LayerNorm vor jedem Sub-Layer anwendet und so den Residual-Pfad sauber hält
  • Sub-Layer 1 (Attention) die Kommunikation zwischen Token übernimmt
  • Sub-Layer 2 (FFN) die Berechnung innerhalb jedes Tokens übernimmt
  • Residual-Verbindungen Informationen bewahren und den Gradientenfluss ermöglichen
  • Eingabe- und Ausgabeform identisch sind, was beliebiges Stapeln ermöglicht

In der nächsten Vorlesung werden wir diese Blöcke verwenden, um die vollständige GPT-Architektur zusammenzusetzen — mit Token-Embeddings, Positions-Embeddings und dem Ausgabeprojektions-Kopf, um ein Modell zu erschaffen, das tatsächlich Text verarbeiten und Vorhersagen erzeugen kann.
